outcome: As of 11 October 2026 I found no accepted proof or refutation that there are infinitely many perfect numbers. The one verified change since 26 January 2024 is GIMPS's 52nd known Mersenne prime (announced 21 October 2024), which adds one even perfect number and does not bear on infinitude. The infinitude claims I found are self-published and unrefereed: one (Vega, 2024) claims finitely many even perfect numbers, and three claim infinitely many Mersenne primes (Catalan-Mersenne preprint, May 2024; Chua Zenodo preprint, January 2026; and Zaman, November 2023, which predates the frozen revision).
problem_asks: Whether the set of all perfect numbers (positive integers n with sigma(n) = 2n) is infinite. Unpacked: (a) the even part: by the Euclid-Euler theorem every even perfect number has the form 2^(p-1)(2^p - 1) with 2^p - 1 prime, so 'infinitely many even perfect numbers' is equivalent to 'infinitely many Mersenne primes', which is open; (b) the odd part: whether any odd perfect number exists and, if one does, whether there are infinitely many. The statement is a single yes/no question about the whole set. An infinite set needs an infinite even part or an infinite odd part, so both parts are asked. The statement does not separately ask for the existence of odd perfect numbers, but that existence question is part (b) of what an infinitude answer depends on.

events.what_happened: GIMPS (volunteer network; discoverer Luke Durant) found the Mersenne prime 2^136279841 - 1, which has 41,024,320 digits. It was first flagged as a probable prime on 11 October 2024 and confirmed by Lucas-Lehmer testing on 12 October 2024. GIMPS announced it on 21 October 2024 and calls it the 52nd known Mersenne prime. It generates the 52nd known even perfect number, 2^136279840 times (2^136279841 - 1). The Wikipedia list records the same exponent, the same 12 October discovery date, and ranks 52 and above as provisional.
events.revisions: None found. Wikipedia dates the discovery to 12 October 2024; the GIMPS press release is dated 21 October 2024, and I have dated the event to the first public statement.
events.delivers: One new finite instance: a 52nd Mersenne prime and so a 52nd known even perfect number. It does not show whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes or even perfect numbers, so it does not move the infinitude question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the even part (infinitely many Mersenne primes) and the odd part (existence and infinitude) are untouched.

checked_by.who: GIMPS volunteer network (Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search)
checked_by.qualification: Distributed computation running repeated Lucas-Lehmer tests; this is machine checking, not a human mathematical reading
checked_by.what_they_did: Ran several definitive Lucas-Lehmer tests on different machines and hardware. The GIMPS release says Mlucas confirmed the prime on 19 October 2024.

machine_checked.system: Lucas-Lehmer primality test, several independent runs (GIMPS release names Mlucas and GPU runs)

events.directly_checkable: The number 2^136279841 - 1 can be tested with the Lucas-Lehmer test. The GIMPS release reports it as prime.
events.direction: Neither for nor against infinitude: it adds one finite instance of the even perfect numbers.
events.object: The Mersenne prime 2^136279841 - 1 (41,024,320 digits) and the even perfect number 2^136279840 times (2^136279841 - 1) it generates. Found by computer search; a specific number confirmed by a primality test.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Note for the Perfect Numbers', EasyChair preprint 13131 (several versions). The abstract says that 'showing that there are finitely many Mersenne primes, we provide a partial answer by proving that is false the infinitude of even perfect numbers', using 'elementary techniques' and properties of the sigma function. It is a claim that the even perfect numbers are finite, resting on a claim that the Mersenne primes are finite. No proof text appears on the pages I read.
events.revisions: Version 1 posted 29 April 2024 (EasyChair page 14Pz). Page sLvl lists versions 1 to 4 with version 4 current and shows version 2 dated 11 July 2024. Page WnQb shows version 3 dated 12 July 2024. A search summary reports a 15 July 2024 date and says the April version said the argument would 'definitively prove' finitude; I did not confirm either point, and the v1 page I read shows the 'partial answer' wording.
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: a negative answer for the even perfect numbers (finitely many), obtained by proving finitely many Mersenne primes. The claim is not verified. It says nothing about odd perfect numbers.
events.remains: The odd part of problem_asks (existence and infinitude of odd perfect numbers) is untouched. The even part is claimed closed negatively but is not established on any page I could read.
events.doubts: (1) The central step, that there are finitely many Mersenne primes, is the open problem itself, and the same abstract calls it open. (2) The abstract says both that the infinitude of Mersenne primes 'remains an open question' and that the paper shows there are finitely many; the page gives no argument that reconciles them. (3) EasyChair preprint with no peer review shown and no disclaimers. (4) The proof text was not reachable; I read only abstract pages. (5) The Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff heuristic predicts infinitely many Mersenne primes; this is a heuristic and not a proof, but it points the other way. I found no public response in searches.
events.direction: Asserts finitude: a negative answer to the even part of the question, via finitude of Mersenne primes.

events.what_happened: 'Hyperbolic Primality Test and Catalan-Mersenne Number Conjecture', Preprints.org manuscript 202405.0952 (version 1, May 2024; the page says it is not peer reviewed). The page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch, so this description comes from search-tool summaries and is unverified. The summaries say it claims infinitely many Mersenne primes by arguing that one double Mersenne prime (M7 is cited) generates an infinite series of Mersenne primes.
events.revisions: Version 1 listed. Later versions not checked.
events.delivers: As claimed: infinitely many Mersenne primes, hence infinitely many even perfect numbers. Unverified. Per the search summaries, the step from one double Mersenne prime to an infinite series is the open problem restated rather than proved.
events.remains: If the claim held, the even part would be settled positively. The odd part is untouched. Not established.
events.doubts: Marked not peer reviewed by Preprints.org. Per a search summary (unverified), the key step is the open problem itself. I could not open the page (HTTP 403).
events.direction: Asserts infinitude of Mersenne primes: a positive answer to the even part if correct.

events.what_happened: Cheong Siong Chua, 'Catalan Mersenne numbers and discovery of the 53rd and 54th Known Mersenne primes', Zenodo preprint (record 18323633, version 1). The abstract claims discovery of the 53rd and 54th known Mersenne primes, 'infinitely many Mersenne primes', and '2 largest prime numbers' with more than 1 billion and 100 million digits. The record says the manuscript was submitted to Inventiones Mathematicae on 24 September 2025 and is 'currently under review'. The record metadata also lists 'Published in: Inventiones Mathematicae, 2026'. The page gives no exponents, no argument, and no verification method. It says the upload timestamps a priority claim for prize money from EFF cooperative awards.
events.revisions: Version 1 only. The Zenodo record was created and published on 21 January 2026. The journal submission date (24 September 2025) is from the abstract. No earlier public posting found.
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: two new Mersenne primes (a 53rd and a 54th) and infinitely many Mersenne primes. If correct, the second claim would imply infinitely many even perfect numbers. Nothing is identified or argued on the page.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks unless the claims are verified. The two claimed primes would need exponents and certificates.
events.directly_checkable: The claimed primes are not identified on the page, so nothing can be checked from it. By digit count, 100 million digits corresponds to an exponent of about 3.3 x 10^8 and 1 billion digits to about 3.3 x 10^9. The lowest untested GIMPS milestone recorded on the Wikipedia list is 141,924,943, so the claimed exponents lie beyond the range GIMPS has tested.
events.doubts: (1) No exponents, no software, no verification method. (2) The stated purpose of the upload is a priority timestamp for prize money, which the abstract says, not a peer review. (3) The status is inconsistent: the abstract says 'currently under review' while the metadata says 'Published in Inventiones Mathematicae, 2026'. (4) The GIMPS list (which I read) has 52 known Mersenne primes, no 53rd, and says ranks 52 and above are provisional. (5) No argument for infinitude is given on the page.
events.direction: Asserts infinitude of Mersenne primes, a positive answer for the even part if correct, and two new Mersenne primes.
events.object: Claimed 53rd and 54th Mersenne primes and two claimed primes of more than 1 billion and about 100 million digits. None is identified on the page, so the object is not checkable from it.

events.what_happened: Budee U. Zaman, 'Infinite Primes, Quadratic Polynomials, and Fermat's Criterion', EasyChair Preprint 11402, posted 28 November 2023. Its abstract says, 'Furthermore, we present a basic argument demonstrating the infinity of Mersenne primes.' The main subject is primes of the form 4(M_p - 2)^2 + 1 under a hypothesis treating Fermat primes as a criterion. The argument is not on the page read.
events.revisions: Version not stated on the page.
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: an elementary argument for infinitely many Mersenne primes, hence infinitely many even perfect numbers. The argument is not visible on the page.
events.remains: The odd part is untouched. The even part would be settled positively if the argument were correct. Not established.
events.doubts: The abstract claims an elementary proof of a famous open problem but the page contains no argument. The abstract text has an extraction gap. The main theorem is hypothesis-based. EasyChair preprint with no peer review shown.
events.direction: Asserts infinitude of Mersenne primes: a positive answer for the even part if correct.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures', Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.2. The abstract reads: 'We discuss two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, an old one and a new one. Heuristic arguments support both conjectures.' The old one is the 1989 New Mersenne Conjecture, per a search summary of the introduction, which I did not read. The new conjecture is not stated in what I read.
events.revisions: Received 1 September 2025; revised 27 September 2025; published 4 December 2025 (JIS). The date given is the journal publication date. A PDF is said to be hosted on the author's Purdue page. I did not check whether it was posted earlier, so the first public date may be earlier.
events.delivers: No proof. Heuristic support for two conjectures about Mersenne numbers. Nothing on whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes is established.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences editorial process
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper after revision (received 1 September 2025, revised 27 September 2025, published 4 December 2025). The acceptance covers the paper's heuristic content, not any claim about infinitude.

events.doubts: The paper gives heuristics only, as its abstract says.
events.direction: Heuristic support for conjectures about Mersenne numbers. No direction on infinitude.

events.what_happened: SeqFan mailing-list thread 'The Mersenne primes as the only sequence records of LPF(2^n - 1)', 3 to 5 September 2026. Tomasz Ordowski proposes the conjecture that Mersenne primes are the only sequence records of the least prime factor of 2^n - 1. DONG HAOXUAN reports partial reductions and no complete proof for the p = 1277 case, and writes that 'the full conjecture would actually imply that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes'. Ordowski restates the implication, and Hasler notes 'it's not yet proven that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes'.
events.delivers: A conjecture, not a proof, and a stated conditional implication: if the conjecture held, it would imply infinitely many Mersenne primes. Neither the conjecture nor the implication is established in the thread.

checked_by.qualification: Named participant; credentials not shown in the thread
checked_by.what_they_did: Checked a bound in DONG HAOXUAN's write-up and stated that the conjecture is not proven

events.doubts: The participants themselves describe the result as conditional or unproven. Ordowski's follow-up says 'there need not be infinitely many Mersenne primes, although heuristics suggest so'.
events.direction: Conditional: an unproven conjecture that would imply infinitude if true. No verdict on the question.

events.what_happened: Tyler Ross, 'A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results', arXiv:2512.04417 (version 1, submitted 4 December 2025). It introduces S-perfect numbers, integers equal to a weighted sum of their proper divisors with weights from a fixed set S. The abstract claims infinitely many {0,m}- and {-1,m}-perfect numbers and characterisations of some {-1,m}-perfect numbers. A search summary says the body states the infinitude of perfect numbers is open. The abstract does not say so, and I could not decode the PDF.
events.delivers: Results about S-perfect numbers, a generalisation. These are not the ordinary perfect numbers in the problem, so they settle nothing here.
events.direction: An analogue. It cuts nowhere on whether there are infinitely many ordinary perfect numbers.

events.what_happened: Hooshang Saeid-Nia, 'There Are No Odd Perfect Numbers', arXiv:2101.07176. The abstract says that 'the existence or non-existence of odd perfect numbers is still an open problem' and 'We address this problem and prove that if a natural number is odd, then it's not perfect.' The arXiv page shows no comments, errata, or peer-review status.
events.revisions: v2 1 April 2021; v3 11 March 2023; v4 17 March 2023 (current).
events.delivers: As claimed: no odd perfect numbers. If correct, every perfect number is even, so the infinitude question reduces to infinitely many Mersenne primes. Claim only; no acceptance shown.
events.remains: The even part (infinitely many Mersenne primes) is untouched.
events.doubts: The arXiv page shows no review status or comments. I read the abstract only and did not read the proof. 'No engagement' means only that my searches found none.
events.direction: Claims that odd perfect numbers do not exist, which would answer the odd part of the question negatively if correct.

events.what_happened: Pascal Ochem and Joshua Zelinsky, 'On odd perfect numbers with exactly one even exponent greater than 2', arXiv:2607.19746 (version 1, submitted 22 July 2026). The abstract reads: 'We show that if all the even exponents of an odd perfect number N are equal to 2 except for one, then 3^{23,000,000,000} divides N.' The abstract page does not mention any AI system. The PDF body was unreadable to my fetch.
events.delivers: A divisibility constraint on a restricted class of putative odd perfect numbers. It concerns odd perfect numbers only and says nothing about whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers.
events.direction: Constraint on odd perfect numbers. It cuts nowhere on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Marco Mantovanelli, 'Certified Minimal-Prime Branch Closures for Odd Perfect Numbers', arXiv:2607.04365 (version 1, submitted 5 July 2026, math.GM). The abstract says that for an odd perfect number N with q the least prime divisor, the paper closes the branches q = 5, 7, 11, 13 and 17 by valuation balance, lower-prime avoidance and certificate checks. It says the q = 3 branch and the branches q >= 19 are not addressed, and that the result is not a nonexistence proof. A search summary says a certificate release with Python verifiers is included, which I did not inspect. A search summary also reports an acknowledgement crediting ChatGPT 5.5 with typesetting, literature search and coding help. I could not confirm that in the readable text: the HTML fetch of both halves found no AI disclosure, and the PDF was unreadable.
events.delivers: Excludes odd perfect numbers whose least prime factor is 5, 7, 11, 13 or 17, as claimed, under the certificate contract. Leaves the q = 3 and q >= 19 cases open and does not decide existence.
events.remains: Odd perfect number existence in general, the q = 3 and q >= 19 cases, and the infinitude question.

machine_checked.system: Python verifier scripts with JSONL certificate bundles, as named in a search summary; not verified in the text I could read

events.directly_checkable: The certificate bundles and verifier scripts are reportedly released. I did not inspect them.
events.doubts: The author states the result is narrow. The verification depends on a stated verifier contract. No peer review seen.
events.direction: Partial exclusion of odd perfect numbers in five minimal-prime branches. It cuts nowhere on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Akira Toyohara, Ye Tao and Siqiong Yao, 'Every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors', arXiv:2608.02066 (version 1, submitted 3 August 2026). The paper claims that any quasiperfect number (sigma(n) = 2n + 1) has at least eight distinct prime factors, improving Hagis and Cohen's 1982 bound of seven. It uses three lemmas, a machine elimination for omega at most 6, and a computation reproduced across seven ledgers. It reports a Lean library with 259 theorems and 'zero sorry', and says it found a coverage gap of 35 feasible exponents in Zemann's 2023 preprint. Code and ledgers are said to be archived by the project, with a public repository in preparation.
events.delivers: For quasiperfect numbers only, if the computation holds: omega(n) at least 8. It says nothing about perfect numbers, even or odd, and nothing about their infinitude.

machine_checked.system: Lean (version not stated in the text I read), plus machine elimination ledgers (seven ledgers, CPU and GPU)

events.directly_checkable: The authors say the Lean library and raw ledgers are archived and available on request. The repository was not public when I read the paper. I did not check the Lean code.
events.doubts: Single preprint with no review. The claimed gap in Zemann's code rests on the authors' audit alone. The code is not yet public. Its Lean 'zero sorry' statement is the authors' claim, which I did not verify.
events.direction: A bound for quasiperfect numbers, a neighbouring problem. It cuts nowhere on whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers.

systems.name: Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, AI systems 'carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations, ran the independent verification ledgers, and drafted the text'. The authors say 'the mathematics and computation reported in this paper were produced in an AI-assisted workflow' and that the human authors 'directed the campaign, made the methodological and editorial decisions, reviewed the results'. Ledger 2 'was driven by a different model' (unnamed), and the paper refers to 'two model families' (unnamed).
systems.basis_quote: AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series, orchestrated in a multi-agent branch-synthesize-drill workflow with mandatory machine verification) carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations, ran the independent verification ledgers, and drafted the text.

ai.disclosed_cost: Section 5.8, 'Computing resources, timeline, and the seven independent ledgers', exists in the paper. I did not read it, so no cost is recorded.

disputes.summary: Vega (EasyChair, 2024) claims there are finitely many even perfect numbers, via finitely many Mersenne primes. Zaman (2023), the Catalan-Mersenne Preprints.org paper (2024) and Chua (Zenodo, 2026) claim infinitely many Mersenne primes. None is accepted by specialists in the sources I read, and the claims are not adjudicated here.

summary: Searches (44 queries) and about 20 opened pages found no accepted result on whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers, and none since 26 January 2024. Euclid-Euler makes the even part equivalent to infinitely many Mersenne primes, which Wikipedia (opened) lists as unknown, and the odd part (existence and infinitude) is also open per Wikipedia. The official record is GIMPS's 52nd known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841 - 1, announced 21 October 2024; it adds one finite even perfect number and I have recorded it as an instance, not as movement of the infinitude question. The Wikipedia list (opened) says the 51st exponent was verified exhaustively and ranks 52 and above are provisional, with no 53rd prime listed. The infinitude claims since January 2024 are: Vega (April and July 2024, finitude; the page I read gives the partial-answer wording, and I could not confirm the 'definitively' wording a search summary attributes to v1); a Catalan-Mersenne Preprints.org preprint (May 2024, infinitude; page returned 403, so only search summaries describe it); and Chua (Zenodo, 21 January 2026, infinitude plus a 53rd and 54th Mersenne prime, with no exponents or argument on the page). Zaman's 2023 EasyChair note, which predates the window, also claims an elementary proof of infinitude of Mersenne primes; the argument is not on its page. None of these has a checkable public argument or specialist engagement that I could find. Two close calls: whether the 52nd-prime event should count toward the question (I record it as a finite instance, which seems to fall under the scope rule), and whether the Chua claims, which would be new Mersenne primes beyond GIMPS's tested range, should count if true (I record them as claims). Adjacent results: the quasiperfect bound of eight prime factors (Toyohara, Tao and Yao, August 2026) credits Anthropic's Claude with load-bearing work per the authors' acknowledgements; it is a different problem and is recorded as discounted. Odd-perfect results (Mantovanelli and Ochem-Zelinsky, July 2026; Saeid-Nia 2021 claim of no odd perfect numbers) are recorded as discounted because they concern existence, not infinitude. The AI search (per the DEEP_DIVE requirement) found no AI-credited result on perfect numbers themselves. Searches over OpenAI's openai/math README (families named there are not perfect-number ones), the Anthropic Fable and Mythos announcements, and general AI-math trackers gave no perfect-number entry. A blog post reports that chatbots (Claude, Gemini) affirmed a 'new perfect number' that was false; it is not a published claim and is not recorded as an event. The Mantovanelli paper's ChatGPT 5.5 acknowledgement is reported in a search summary but I could not confirm it in readable text, so no system is recorded for it.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a larger 'moved' count: the 52nd Mersenne prime and the Chua claim of a 53rd and 54th (if true) each add to the known list of even perfect numbers, and a reader who counts any new instance as progress would record the 2024 event as a change in status. The strongest case against any settlement: every infinitude or finitude claim I found is either unverified (Vega, Catalan-Mersenne, Zaman, Chua) or conditional (seqfan 2026), and the Vega and Chua claims contradict each other and the heuristic direction. On the odd side, Saeid-Nia's 2021 claim of no odd perfect numbers, if it held, would not settle infinitude because it reduces the question to Mersenne primes rather than answering it.
what_would_settle_it: A proof, accepted by specialists in a refereed venue, that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes (or finitely many). For the Chua claim: the exponents of the 53rd and 54th primes and a Lucas-Lehmer certificate that can be rerun. For Vega: the proof text and a referee report on whether 'finitely many Mersenne primes' is established. For the odd part: a proof of nonexistence or an explicit odd perfect number, which would change the even and odd parts but not by itself settle infinitude.

events.credibility_reason: Claims finitude of Mersenne primes (a landmark) by 'elementary techniques' while the same abstract calls it open; self-contradictory abstract, unrefereed EasyChair venue, four versions within weeks, no expert uptake in ~2.5 years, and the claimed direction runs against the standard heuristic.

Landmark claim (infinitely many Mersenne primes) with no uptake in ~29 months; unrefereed, anonymous in the record, and the reported key step restates the open problem; the page itself could not be opened.

No argument and no exponents given; upload framed as a prize-priority timestamp; inconsistent publication status (under review vs published in Inventiones); claimed primes lie far beyond GIMPS's tested range and GIMPS lists no 53rd; no uptake.
A 'basic argument' for infinitude of Mersenne primes tacked onto a hypothesis-based note on an unrefereed EasyChair preprint, with no uptake in nearly three years.

Claimed nonexistence of odd perfect numbers (a landmark) with no uptake in nearly six years, repeated revisions, and the field continuing to publish odd-perfect constraints (e.g. Ochem-Zelinsky 2026) as if open.

events.ai_basis: AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series, orchestrated in a multi-agent branch-synthesize-drill workflow with mandatory machine verification) carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations, ran the independent verification ledgers, and drafted the text.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether the set of perfect numbers is infinite. Infinitely many Mersenne primes would answer it in full (yes), so the Catalan-Mersenne, Chua and Zaman claims are scored whole; finitude of even perfect numbers (Vega) leaves the odd part open, and nonexistence of odd perfect numbers (Saeid-Nia) settles only the odd restriction, so both are case. All five are set aside as not_credible: each is a landmark claim on an unrefereed or self-archive venue, with no uptake over years, and each has its own red flags (self-contradictory abstract, no argument or exponents, prize-priority framing, a key step that restates the problem). The 52nd Mersenne prime is one more finite instance. Odd-perfect constraints (Ochem-Zelinsky, Mantovanelli) narrow where an odd perfect number could exist but bound nothing on infinitude, so they are none. Wagstaff and the SeqFan thread offer heuristics and conditional conjectures (none), and Ross and the quasiperfect paper address changed questions (variant). The quasiperfect paper's quote credits Claude with discovering and proving the lemmas, so its own row is generated, but it is a variant and carries no weight here.
judgement.doubts: Mantovanelli's reported ChatGPT 5.5 acknowledgement (typesetting, literature search, coding) was unconfirmed and would be none anyway. Several preprints.org claims (403) and other infinitude claims listed in 'incomplete' were never opened. Saeid-Nia could be read as none (a reduction) rather than case; it makes no difference because it is pre-snapshot and not credible.
